title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
summary: Embedded payloads hide the real malicious content inside a second, apparently harmless file. The carrier is usually a document, script, installer or signed binary that already looks normal on the endpoint, while the code that matters sits in an overlay appended past the end of the carrier, in an unused metadata field, or nestled inside a file of the same type. Because the outer file keeps its familiar extension, icon and digital signature, allowlisting and signature checks still pass, and a scanner that only inspects the outer format sees nothing unusual. The artefact defenders can work with is structural rather than behavioural: a file whose size or section layout does not match the vendor baseline, a mismatched internal hash, executable bytes in a region that should hold padding, or an unexpected child process that pulls content out of the carrier. Distinguishing hostile embedding from legitimate embedding comes down to context. Software installers, self-extracting archives and updaters also carry nested binaries, so the useful pivot is whether the embedded content is later written to disk, mapped or injected into a process, and whether the parent process has any business doing so.

beginner.definition: An embedded payload is extra hidden content carried inside a normal-looking file. The outer file may be a document, a script or a program. The hidden part is the real malicious code. This is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information, which covers ways of hiding content from security tools. The outer file often stays valid and signed, so nothing looks wrong at first glance.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your security tools check the outer file type, so hidden content can slip past them. A signed program can carry added code and still pass a signature check. Filters that block executables may allow a document that hides one inside. This means a file that looks familiar is not proof that it is safe. You need to look inside files, not just at their names.
howItWorks: An attacker takes a normal file, such as a document, installer or trusted program, as the carrier.
They attach their hidden code to the end of that file, in a region called an overlay.
They may instead nest a script or program inside another file of the same type.
The carrier opens normally, so the user sees expected behaviour and trusts the file.
When the carrier runs, it copies, decodes or launches the hidden code.
That hidden code often arrives through macros, script engines or injection into a running process.
beginner.example: Picture a postal box that only checks the shape of the envelope. A letter inside holds a second, smaller letter sealed in its own envelope. The post office weighs the outer envelope, sees a normal letter, and passes it on. The person who opens the first envelope finds the second one, which nobody inspected. If the sender also used an official, stamped envelope, the sorting office trusts it even more and looks no further.
takeaways: A familiar file type or a valid signature does not prove that the file contains only what it claims.
Compare file size and structure with a known-good copy, because hidden content usually changes one of them.
Watch what document readers, installers and script hosts launch, since that is when the hidden part runs.

objectives: Explain how embedding a payload inside a benign carrier defeats content filters and signature checks.
Describe common ways content is embedded, including overlays, unused metadata fields and same-type nesting.
Identify structural artefacts such as size mismatches, appended data and high entropy regions that indicate hidden content.
Distinguish malicious embedding from legitimate embedded content in installers, updaters and self-extracting archives.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from Steganography and what defenders should monitor at execution time.
